misconceptions: let and const are not hoisted
Arrow functions have their own this
JavaScript classes work like Java classes

templates.question: What is a closure in JavaScript? Give a practical use, and explain the classic bug of creating functions in a for loop declared with var.
keyPoints: A closure is a function together with the variables of the scope it was created in, which stay alive as long as the function does
Closures give private state, factories, partial application and event handlers that remember their context
With var there is one variable for the whole function, shared by every iteration, so every callback sees its final value
let creates a new binding for each iteration, which fixes the loop

templates.question: What is hoisting? How do var, let, const and function declarations behave when they are used before their declaration?
keyPoints: Declarations are processed before the code of their scope runs
var is hoisted and initialised to undefined
let and const are hoisted but stay uninitialised until their declaration (the temporal dead zone); using them earlier throws a ReferenceError
A function declaration is hoisted with its body; a function expression follows the rules of its variable
let and const are block-scoped, var is function-scoped

templates.question: How is the value of this determined in JavaScript, and why do arrow functions behave differently?
keyPoints: this depends on how a function is called: obj.method() gives obj
A plain call gives undefined in strict mode (the global object otherwise); new gives the new object
call, apply and bind set this explicitly
Arrow functions have no this of their own; they use the this of the enclosing scope
Passing obj.method as a callback loses its this unless it is bound

templates.question: How does prototypal inheritance work, and what does the class keyword do under the hood?
keyPoints: Every object has an internal link to a prototype object
A property lookup walks up the prototype chain until it finds the property or reaches null
Methods defined on the prototype are shared by all instances
class is syntax over constructor functions and prototypes: methods go on Class.prototype, extends links the prototypes, super calls the parent
Object.create creates an object with a given prototype

templates.question: The check if (count == false) is true when count is 0 and also when it is an empty string, and [] == false is true as well. Why, and what should the code do instead?
keyPoints: == converts both operands to a common type before comparing: false, '' and [] all become 0
=== compares type and value without conversion
Use === and convert explicitly when a conversion is intended
0, '', null, undefined, NaN and false are falsy; NaN is not equal to itself, so use Number.isNaN

templates.question: A function receives a settings object, changes one property and returns it. Later another part of the app shows the changed value unexpectedly. Explain why, and how you would avoid it.
keyPoints: Objects are passed as a copy of the reference, so changing the parameter's properties changes the caller's object
Primitives are copied by value
const prevents reassignment, not mutation
Return a new object instead, for example { ...settings, theme: 'dark' }
Spread copies only one level; structuredClone makes a deep copy

misconceptions: async functions run on a separate thread
Promise.all cancels the other promises when one of them rejects

templates.question: How does the JavaScript event loop work? Why does a long synchronous loop freeze the page?
keyPoints: JavaScript runs on one thread with one call stack
Timers, network and I/O are handled by the environment, which queues their callbacks as tasks
When the stack is empty the event loop runs the next task; after every task all queued microtasks (promise callbacks) run
A long synchronous computation keeps the stack busy, so no events, timers or rendering can happen
Move heavy work to a Web Worker (or a worker thread in Node) or split it into chunks

templates.question: In which order is this logged, and why: console.log('A'); setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C')); console.log('D');
keyPoints: A and D are logged first, because they run synchronously
C comes next: the promise callback is a microtask, run as soon as the call stack is empty
B comes last: the timer callback is a task that runs in a later turn of the event loop
The output is A, D, C, B; all microtasks run before the next task

templates.question: A page needs data from three independent APIs. How would you request it, and how does your choice behave when one request fails?
keyPoints: Start all three requests before awaiting, and await Promise.all, so the total time is that of the slowest call
Awaiting each call in turn makes them sequential and adds their times up
Promise.all rejects as soon as one promise rejects; the other requests keep running and their results are discarded
Promise.allSettled returns every outcome, so the page can show partial data
Add timeouts or an AbortController

templates.question: Inside items.forEach(async item => { await save(item) }), the code after the loop runs before the saves finish, and failed saves are not caught by the surrounding try/catch. Why?
keyPoints: forEach ignores the promises returned by its callback and does not wait for them
The surrounding function continues at once, so its try/catch is no longer around the saves
Rejections nobody awaits become unhandled
Use for...of with await for sequential saves, or await Promise.all(items.map(save)) for concurrent ones

templates.question: How do you cancel a fetch request in flight, or give it a timeout, in JavaScript?
keyPoints: Pass an AbortController's signal to fetch and call abort(); the fetch promise rejects with an AbortError
AbortSignal.timeout(ms) creates a signal for a timeout, and AbortSignal.any combines signals
Promises themselves cannot be cancelled: the API must accept a signal
In a React effect, abort in the cleanup function
